title: About
text:
This blog contains five “mini-projects” that were completed over the course of a semester taking STAT-326: Mathematical Statistics. Over the course of the semester, the mini-projects looked into sampling distributions, estimation, confidence intervals, Bayesian Statistics, and the use of p-values. Below are some brief summaries/reflections on each of the five summaries that provide context into each post in the blog.
Mini Project 1: Sampling Distribution of the Sample Minimum and Sample Maximum:
In this project, we looked into sample statistics and how the Central Limit Theorem and different probability distributions affect sample statistics such as the sample maximum and the sample minimum, along with standard error of those two statistics. A nice way this project tied in with other projects is that it set us up for simulation in R. Which came in very handy with Project 3’s confidence intervals. Furthermore, looking into how different distributions have different “spreads” which ties into “average width” of Project 3. My biggest takeaway from this mini-project is that the Central Limit Theorem does not apply to every sample statistic.
Mini Project 2: “A Meaningful Story”
In this project, the main focus was on the topic of estimators. However, instead of doing a whole coding/simulation style project, a creative short story using topics in our “Estimators” unit was written. This story is based on a true story about the time that I drove home through the Adirondacks in a blizzard and a travel ban. Throughout the story there are many not so subtle references to estimators, variance, bias, and likelihood among other key words. My biggest takeaway from this project is that it allowed students to really understand estimators in a more “real world” way as opposed to a bunch of numbers on paper and lines of code in R.
Mini Project 3: Simulation to Investigate Confidence Intervals
This project had students look into how different parameters in the confidence interval formula affect coverage rate and average width of a confidence interval. Two main parameters were looked at, \(\hat{p}\), and population size, \(n\). Through simulation students were able to see the rate at which each confidence interval covered a point estimate and the average width of each confidence interval, and how different \(\hat{p}\) and \(n\), affect these. This project ties in nicely with both mini project 1 and 4 due to the amount of simulation performed and it tied in quite nicely to mini project 5 which had students look into p-values on a deeper level, especially since in Stat 113 students can use confidence intervals to help determine whether or not to reject the null hypothesis. My Biggest takeaway is that at small \(n\) and \(\hat{p}\) close to 0.5, the “Large Sample Assumption” does not hold.
Mini Project 4: Bayesian Analysis
In Mini Project 4, students looked into how 3 different priors, 2 informative and 1 uninformative can affect how we predict the number of proportion of points that Rafael Nadal scores given he is serving. This was a great way to look into how Bayesian statistics differ from frequentest statistics. We essentially took everything learnt from the unit and put it into a simulation project. This tied in quite nicely into projects 1 and 3 based off of the shear amount of simulation. However, we also got to see how Bayesian statistics can predict based off of human knowledge and how we can use more understandable “Credible Intervals”. My biggest takeaway from this project is almost two-fold. I love the way that background knowledge of a certain topic could and should be used when looking into prediction. However, I believe this should be used predominantly by field experts, as “informative” priors by someone who is relatively “uninformed” seem sort of untrustworthy.
Mini Project 5: Advantages and Drawbacks of Using p-values
This project had students read an article titled Moving to a World Beyond \(p<0.05\). This article looked into how the world of statistics shouldn’t be ruled by p-values, and that thoughtful thinking and background knowledge should be used when making statements about statistics. This nicely ties into the class as unit 5 was all about hypothesis testing, and this project allowed students to get some introspect into the drawbacks of what we were learning and not to just take things for whether its p-value is less than 0.05 or not. This really ties into project 3 with confidence intervals as the paper explicitly mentions them as a source of confusion to the general public, and it details how we should talk about them in general. The biggest takeaway from this is that no matter the p-value, no “significance” is still significant, and that non “significant” results should still be published as learning material for future researchers.

title: Mini Project 3: Simulation to Investigate Confidence Intervals
text:
“I have followed all rules for collaboration for this project, and I have not used generative AI on this project.” - Alex Tidd

library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(ggplot2)
library(resample)

For the three population sizes we will be using n1 = 5, n2 = 50, and n3 = 5000. For the two population proportions, we will use p1 = 0.45 and p2 = 0.9.

## creating a function using Dr. Higham's code from lab 3.2

generate_samp_prop <- function(n, p) {
  x <- rbinom(1, n, p) # randomly generate number of successes for the sample
  
  ## number of successes divided by sample size
  phat <- x / n
  lb <- phat - qt(0.95, n-1) * sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
  ub <- phat + qt(0.95, n-1) * sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
  
  prop_df <- tibble(phat, lb, ub)
  
  return(prop_df)
}

Creating 5000 sample proportions and 5000 associated CIs for n = 5000 and p = 0.45 and finding coverage rate and average width.

## Code from Dr. Higham's Lab 3.1
generate_samp_prop(5000, 0.45)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
   phat    lb    ub
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 0.454 0.443 0.466

n_sim <- 5000

prop_ci_df_large_near <- map(1:n_sim, 
    \(i) generate_samp_prop(5000, 0.45)) |>
  bind_rows()

## finding coverage rate and avg width using code provided in Dr. Higham's Lab 3.2
prop_ci_df_large_near <- prop_ci_df_large_near |>
  mutate(ci_width = ub - lb,
         ci_cover_ind = if_else(0.45 > lb & 0.45 < ub,
                                true = 1,
                                false = 0)) |>
  summarise(avg_width = mean(ci_width),
            coverage_rate = mean(ci_cover_ind))

prop_ci_df_large_near

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  avg_width coverage_rate
      <dbl>         <dbl>
1    0.0231         0.894

So, here we see that in three cases, our assumption of large sample does not hold, which matches our first table of results.
Discussion:
For this simulation of confidence intervals, sample size, n, was varied between 5, 50, and 5000. Furthermore our p_hat, was varied between 0.45 and 0.9. In order to see how the large sample assumption holds for assymptotic confidence intervals of proportion, average width of confidence interval and coverage rate of confidence interval was found.
In order to test this, expected results are as follws: As p_hat approaches 0.5, we should see the largest average width compared with average witdth of same sample size, and as n is increased, we should see a decrease in average width, when p_hat is held constant. This is because our width parameter is defined as: \[\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\] Furthermore, we expect coverage rate to stay the same throughout this simulation as that is solely depended on our confidence level. The only time this should change is when confidence level is adjusted, which in this experiment, it remains at 90%. So in this case coverage rate should be around 0.9.
The results in this experiment followed theory to a tee. When using the “Wald” interval for confidence interval of a proportion, you must make sure the np > 10 and n(1 - p) > 10 for our assumptions to hold. In this case, 3 of the 6 intervals tested upheld this stipulation, n = 5000 and p = 0.45, n = 5000 and p = 0.9, and n = 50 and p = 0.45.
In the case of n = 5000, we see that when p = 0.45, the average width was roughly 0.0231 compared to when p = 0.9 at average width roughly 0.0140. This follows what we expect as when n is held constant, p further from 0.5 will have a smaller average width. Furthermore, the average widths of n = 5000 we’re also the smallest when p is held constant, like we expect. And for both n = 5000, coverage rate is approximately 0.9.
In the case of n = 50, our assumption only holds when p = 0.45. We see a smaller average width when p = 0.9, as expected. However, coverage rate is only approximately 0.9 when p = 0.45. This is as expected since when n = 50 and p = 0.9, the stipulation of n(1 - p) > 10 is not upheld. So we see that when n is mid-sized, the large sample assumption is only upheald when p is close to 0.5.
Lastly, small n. When n = 5, we see that neither np > 10 nor n(1 - p) > 10 is upheld. The results of this simulation reflect this. The average widths followed our expected pattern, however the widths 0.819 for p = 0.45 and 0.324 for p = 0.9, which are very large widths and don’t really tell you anything since proportions can only be between 0 and 1. So a width of 0.8 is basically like saying “we’re 90% confident it could be anywhere”. And lastly, the coverage rates were approximately 0.93 for p = 0.45 and 0.39 for n = 0.9. Which essientiall means for p = 0.9 we wanted a 90% confidence interval and only came away with a 40% confidence interval. And comparing that to an average with of 0.324 being only a 40% confidence level, a 90% confidence interval would have very large bounds, running into the same issue as n = 5 and p = 0.45, where the confidence interval really only tells you that it is somewhere.

title: Mini Project 2: A Meaningful Story
text:
Up in the Northeast corner of New York lies a place no more polar than St. Lawrence County. From the bright, warm, and breezy springtime to the sweltering, Sahara-like summers, and finally to the frigid, dank, and sterile winters, there is no crazier county in the state.
Nestled in this large county, the largest in the state might I add, lies four accredited universities, St. Lawrence University, a small liberal arts college, that for no reason at all has an incredibly strong math department. Clarkson University, an engineering school that prides itself on claiming that their school “actually gets people hired” (when challenged with the argument that SLU has the 2nd best alumni network in the country amongst private schools, they revert to saying that at least their getting a BS. When challenged with, “So am I”, there is no rebuttal). Then there’s SUNY Potsdam, a school that is literally only being kept afloat by its music program. And finally, SUNY Canton, consistently described as “a university”.
What keeps these four schools together as one “big family” is the fact that each school is well equipped and extremely familiar with the snow. There is simply no such thing as “schoolwide class closure due to inclement weather”. Some (I) have experienced walking to CHEM 222 with frozen tears in -30 degree weather (243 K). Those tears quickly unfreeze and start pouring when the students are made aware that schools like the University of Tennessee closing due to an inch of snow. This was soon about to change.
One day a St. Lawrence student, Alex, was going to Waltham, MA to visit his younger brother, Brendan, at his place of higher education, Bentley University, where he studies accounting. Before heading down to the Boston area, Alex’s CS 140 professor, Dr. Choong-Soo Lee, made him aware that he should leave on Wednesday, the day before a massive snowstorm. Alex, an experienced snow driver, hailing from Rochester, NY, disregarded this advice since he knows that when it comes to weather apps, he feels like predicted snowfall is consistently biased-high, and feels like he’ll be able to manage in his 2018 Jeep Grand Cherokee equipped with BFGoodrich All-Terrain T/A KO3 tires. And managed he did. He also noted that in fact the actual snowfall was less than estimated, biased-high, some statisticians might say.
Upon arriving at Bentley and spending time with brother, Alex expressed his desire to return to St. Lawrence on Sunday. “OH NO!” expressed his brother Brendan. Alex was bewildered with this statement, did his brother want him to spend more quality time with him, yes, as Alex would too, but his voice seemed too concerned for that to be the case. Brendan continued, “There’s going to be a massive snowstorm Sunday in the Northeast! Bentley has already cancelled class Monday”.
Alex, in all of his infinite wisdom and confidence arrogantly stated: “Pfft in all my four years at St. Lawrence, not once have I had a snow day! It simply doesn’t exist in North Country School Vocab. Besides, the estimators used by the weather app are all biased high”. Brendan challenged Alex on this statement and an intense statistics battle broke out (talk about a thesis defense). Brendan started the argument: Alex lets first consider the northeast, snowfall is most likely going to normally distributed here, let snowfall be a random variable, this means that the weather apps expected snowfall of 3ft is the mean! You’re gonna get hit with three ft of snow overnight! Alex rebuts: Brendan, that is the entire Northeast. Let’s just take a sample of that and make a sampling distribution of the mean snowfalls of schools in my area: SUNY Potsdam, SUNY Canton, St. Lawrence, and Clarkson, and for good measure, we’ll throw in Paul Smith’s University as well, since this is what I’m going to drive through (please note that in a real sampling distribution these places would be chosen at random). Brendan, this sample mean is legitimately 1 foot. That is light work. Furthermore, the weather app finds its snowfall estimator using the Maximum Likelihood Estimator. A method of finding an estimator based off maximizing the likelihood of an estimator using calculus but neglected to find the methods of moments estimator even though the MLE is biased (at least in my experience with weather prediction)!!! “SO BOOM I WIN” exclaimed Alex, citing his educational superiority over a measly accounting major at a business school. But Alex was about to find out just how wrong he was.
After waking up, seeing that the four North Country Universities had cancelled classes (for like the first time ever), and deciding to not check his phone to see a St. Lawrence County travel ban, Alex found himself ripping up I-90W to I-87N. Alex entered the stretch of I-87N that enters the Adirondack State Park. He found himself on an unplowed stretch of interstate going 40 MPH behind a semi. “Maybe Brendan was right” he thought. Then, stupidly and arrogantly, he got off at exit 26, Pottersville-Minerva, NY. The situation quickly got serious. Alex was driving through the Adirondacks in a blizzard over unplowed roads with like 3ft of snow on the ground. Then Alex realized “OH NO I FORGOT TO TAKE VARIENCE INTO CONSIDERATION!”. Alex quickly realized to things, 1) His “Sampling distribution” was not done properly (it was not a bunch of random samples, instead he handpicked 5 random cases and only took one simulation of it), and 2) He did not use the var() function in R. Alex realized his small sample size had a HUGE variance and that 3ft of snow, even though not the expected value, was within the range of the variance of the distribution. Alex thought to himself “Dr. Higham is going to kill me” and “Brendan, my kid brother, was right and I should’ve listened to him”.
After all the driving and 32oz of RedBull later (divided into one 20oz can and one 12oz can), Alex made it back to Canton safely and learnt that in order to do well in statistics, you actually need to understand what a sampling distribution is. He also learnt that he probably shouldn’t travel through the dacks when there is a travel ban (Don’t worry he had an unopened Army MRE on him, as well as an army sleeping bag and 1L of water in his Nalgene).

title: Mini Project 5: Advantages and Drawbacks of Using p-values
text:
Question 1:
To me, I understand this quote to mean that the further away we get from blindly saying “p < 0.05 Reject the null” the more we start thinking deeper into what we are studying and stating. I think a big example of this is in time-based sports. A sport like cycling, 1 second can mean the difference between first and 10th. However, a certain piece of equipment, or a new body position can cut seconds down but, may not cut time down drastically enough for a p < 0.05. Thinking statistically would be realizing that even the p-value isn’t low this change is actually relevant in its context, and looking into other statistics in the sport can allow us to gain a better understanding of its context. It’s looking at the big picture instead of homing in on one small detail.
Question 2:
Essentially, what the authors are trying to say is that adding the term “statistically significant” confuses the true meaning of what the statistics are saying. As the authors note, “statistically significant” was originally coined to indicate which results to investigate further. However, the general public, both statistically inclined and not, take this to mean the result is significant and to take it at face value. It also adds confusion when paired with “p < 0.05” as now both terms are intertwined, so someone will see “p < 0.05” and instantly go to “statistically significant” and vice versa. The phrase has lost its true meaning.
Question 3:
I wholly agree with this statement. In my time in other fields such as chemistry, I have heard time and time again that “No ‘significant’ data is still data”. An example of this: A student wants to see if a certain catalyst has a “significant” impact on reaction rate, it does not. The student should not throw his research out or hide this result from his write up, but, put it in there as a) their threshold is arbitrary, and b) there is still a lot of information one can extrapolate from a result not passing a certain “threshold”. Data published should be based on if the data is relevant to the research and if information can be learnt from the data and used by future researchers to aid in their research, like; maybe this one catalyst doesn’t have much effect on rate.
Question 4:
I do agree with this statement, even though it did take me a bit to make up my mind on it. In the future we may see a new accepted standard, but the field of statistics is ever evolving so new ideas will keep being accepted and tweaks to new models will always be made. Furthermore, what is “important” to one statistician may not be “important” to another. Frankly, I am a big fan of the “Second Generation P-Value” (SGPV) by Blume et al. since the test is very easy to understand and that conclusion statements written with this test can have little confusion to the general public. The 0 to 1 approach with 0.5 being completely inconclusive is very straight forward, something I hold very important.
Question 5:
In general, I think “statistical thoughtfulness” is looking at the grand scheme of your work before starting and definitely before concluding things. As I touched on in question 1, knowing the context about the topic you are studying and how some value that aren’t p < 0.05 are actually pretty significant. It also plays a role in deciding on what you use as estimators, as the authors say. A really good example of this is my SYE where I had an optimized set of parameters that greatly lowered a mean residual value. However, these parameters allowed for negative rankings and win probabilities around 6 x 10-6 which isn’t really realistic at all, even though it may be, as some may claim, “significant”. Always research before going in and don’t go looking for specific data as it may be misleading.
Question 6:
I believe that these authors believe the big problem stems around the confusion around the term “significant” and “confident”. It is much more straightforward to use percentages to describe how much the data aligns with the hypothesis, which is honestly way more straightforward and actually feels more descriptive in what the data is showing. Frankly, I don’t think slapping a new name on it will help. I think the best way to solve this issue is by simply describing the data differently as shown in the reading: “Goodman says investigators might add a statement such as “There is an 80% chance that this drug raises the risk, and a 60% chance that the risk is at least doubled.” (Wasserstein, 5).
Question 7:
“If it were easy, it would have already been done, because as we have noted, this is nowhere near the first time the alarm has been sounded.” Start of section 5 on page 8. I personally love this quote as it shows just how deep p-values have been ingrained in all fields. And how it has almost become industry standard in many fields. It sort of proves my point that I have stood by since freshman year that a lot of researchers in other fields (predominantly biologists), don’t have a deep understanding of what their testing in a statistical test, as they are huge p < 0.05 people. It shows that entire fields need to be better educated in statistical modeling and have to be on board with changing their scientific methods and looking back at old research and rethinking conclusions written based off of p < 0.05, which would take a lot of work.

title: Mini Project 4: Bayesian Analysis
text:
library(mosaic)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

In this project, we will be looking at how informed vs non-informed Bayesian distributions can predict the proportion of Tennis legend Rafa Nada, points won off of his own serves. We will look into two informed models and one informed model, and pick which model we would use to predict this proportion.
First lets start with the prior that Dr. Higham has provided a nice code template for a gamma distribution

## Informed Gamma

## trying to get a prb of 0.75 and a probability
## that lambda is less than 0.7 equal to 0.02

## informative prior for 0.75 wins and certain of no less than 0.7
alphas <- seq(0.01, 10000, length.out = 200000) 
ks <- alphas / 0.75

target_prob <- 0.02
prob_less_0.7 <- pgamma(0.7, alphas, ks)

tibble(alphas, ks, prob_less_0.7) |>
  mutate(close_to_target = abs(prob_less_0.7 - target_prob)) |>
  filter(close_to_target == min(close_to_target))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  alphas    ks prob_less_0.7 close_to_target
   <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>           <dbl>
1   916. 1222.        0.0200     0.000000451

## we see that an alpha of 916 and k = 1222 gets us closest to this target

Now lets try another informative prior. I’m going to try a beta distribution since the data is binomial, either Nadal wins the point on his own serve, or he does not, and the events are independant (assuming), and lastly we are dealing with proportions and beta uses quantities between 0 and 1! This gives us a nice beta distribution and will be a lovely conjugate prior!

## Informed Beta

## Trying to simulate to find best prior alpha and beta 

target_prb_b <- 46/66

alphas_b <- seq(0.1, 1000, length.out = 50000)
betas_b <- ((1 - 46/66) * alphas_b) / (46/66)

param_df <- tibble(alphas_b, betas_b)
param_df <- param_df |> mutate(vars = (alphas_b * betas_b) / ((alphas_b + betas_b)^2 * (alphas_b + betas_b + 1)))


target_var_b <- 0.05657^2

param_df <- param_df |> mutate(dist_to_target = abs(vars - target_var_b))

## We find that the informed beta prior is beta(45.3, 19.7)

Time for an uniformed prior: A reasonable uniformed would be a uniform 0 to 1, or in otherwords a beta(1,1)!
Now that we have the three priors, lets plot them!

ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

gamma_prior = dgamma(ps, 916, 1222)
beta_prior = dbeta(ps, 45.3, 19.7)
noninform_prior = dbeta(ps, 1, 1)

plot_prior_df <- tibble(ps, gamma_prior, beta_prior, noninform_prior) |>
  pivot_longer(2:4, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("prior_type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = plot_prior_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = prior_type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")








Now, lets update these priors with the data from the 2020 French Open!
Updating our gamma informative prior:

## updating the gamma:
## updating alpha is the sum of yi + old alpha
## updating k is old k + n

## Nadal won 56 of 84. so new alpha = 56 + 916 and new k = 1222 + 84
## Informative post is gamma(972, 1306)

gamma_post = dgamma(ps, 972, 1306)

Updating our informative beta:

## to update a beta distribution, new alpha = yobs + old alpha
## new beta = n - yobs + old beta
## informed posterior is now Beta(101.3, 47.7

beta_post = dbeta(ps, 101.3, 47.7)

Updating our non-informative prior:

## Even though it looks like our distribution is a uniform(0, 1), it is actually a beta(1, 1), this allows us to work with a conjugate prior. So we go through the same steps as our informative beta proir to get the posterior. 

## new alpha = 56 + 1 = 57
## new beta = 84 - 56 + 1 = 29

## uninformed posterior is now a beta(57, 29)

noninform_post = dbeta(ps, 57, 29)

Now lets plot these:

ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

gamma_post = dgamma(ps, 972, 1306)
beta_post = dbeta(ps, 101.3, 47.7)
noninform_post = dbeta(ps, 57, 29)

plot_post_df <- tibble(ps, gamma_post, beta_post, noninform_post) |>
  pivot_longer(2:4, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("post_type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = plot_post_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = post_type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")








You can’t really do much with this without seeing how they overlay with their respective priors, so lets do that.

ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

gamma_prior = dgamma(ps, 916, 1222)
beta_prior = dbeta(ps, 45.3, 19.7)
noninform_prior = dbeta(ps, 1, 1)
gamma_post = dgamma(ps, 972, 1306)
beta_post = dbeta(ps, 101.3, 47.7)
noninform_post = dbeta(ps, 57, 29)

plot_df <- tibble(ps, gamma_post, beta_post, noninform_post, 
                       gamma_prior, beta_prior, noninform_prior) |>
  pivot_longer(2:7, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = plot_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")








Now lets look at each individually:

## informative gamma
ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

gamma_prior = dgamma(ps, 916, 1222)
gamma_post = dgamma(ps, 972, 1306)

gamma_df <- tibble(ps, gamma_post, gamma_prior) |>
  pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = gamma_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")







## informative beta
ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

beta_prior = dbeta(ps, 45.3, 19.7)
beta_post = dbeta(ps, 101.3, 47.7)

beta_df <- tibble(ps, beta_post, beta_prior) |>
  pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = beta_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")







## non-informative beta
ps <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

noninform_prior = dbeta(ps, 1, 1)
noninform_post = dbeta(ps, 57, 29)

non_df <- tibble(ps, noninform_post, noninform_prior) |>
  pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  separate(distribution, into = c("type", "distribution"))

ggplot(data = non_df, aes(x = ps, y = density, colour = type,
                           linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p")








Before we do any comparisons, it should be not that in all cases, we see a post with a more precise distribution than the prior, meaning our posterior is gethering new information and honing it to a tighter range, which is what we hope to see happens with new information added!
Now, lets look into posterior means:

mean_gamma = 972 / 1306
mean_beta = 101.3 / (101.3 + 47.7)
mean_non = 57 / (57 + 29)

the mean of our informative gamma distribution is 0.7442573, the mean of our informative beta distribution is 0.6798658, and the mean of our non-informative beta posterior is 0.6627907.
Something to note is that the mean of our informative posterior beta and our non-informative posterior beta are very similar. Lets see a 90% credible interval for each.

## Gamma Informative
g_lb = qgamma(0.05, 972, 1306)
g_ub = qgamma(0.95, 972, 1306)

## Our model shows that there is a 90% probability that the proportion of points won by Nadal off of his own serves is between  0.7054313 and 0.7839538

## Beta informative
b_lb = qbeta(0.05, 101.3, 47.7)
b_ub = qbeta(0.95, 101.3, 47.7)

## Our model shows that there is a 90% probability that the proportion of points won by Nadal off of his own serves is between  0.6158332 and 0.7411439

##Non-informative beta
n_lb = qbeta(0.05, 57, 29)
n_ub = qbeta(0.95, 57, 29)

## Our model shows that there is a 90% probability that the proportion of points won by Nadal off of his own serves is between  0.5772453 and 0.7440061

Something interesting to not is that each 90% credible interval contains 0.74 within its bounds, if more data is collected, could we see each distribution start to center around 0.74?
Lets put this all into a table:

Table of Results









Posterior
Posterior Mean
Variance
90% Credible Interval Lower Bound
90% Credible Interval Upper Bound




\(\text{Informative: }Gamma(972, 1306)\)
0.7442573
0.0005698754
0.7054313
0.7839538


\(\text{Informative: } Beta(101.3, 47.7)\)
0.6798658
0.001450989
0.6158332
0.7411439


\(\text{Non - Informative: } Beta(57, 29)\)
0.6627907
0.2209007
0.5772453
0.7440061



We see that each posterior distribution is slightly different from each other. This is true for a multitude of reasons, however this is predominantly because each of these three distributions, we made different assumptions. for the informative gamma, we see that a group of statisticians used a claim that Nadal wins roughly 0.75 of his served points with being certain its no less than 0.7. Whereas our informative beta distribution uses prior knowledge of a previous match, and used a beta distribution due to the binomial nature of the data, and knowledge that we are bounded by 0 and 1. For our non-informative we simply use a uniform(0, 1) / beta(1, 1) distribution. For these reasons we see such differences between the three posteriors.
But a major similarity between the three posteriors is the fact that contained within each of the 90% Credible intervals is 0.74. This leads me to believe that as more information is added, wee will see each of the distributions settle around 0.74.
Based on this if I had to choose a distribution for this data, I’d choose the informative beta distribution. We see that 0.74 is contained in its credible interval, but we also see that it has an extremely low variance. Its variance may not be as low as our informative gamma distribution (0.0005698754), but I like the fact that this informative beta distribution is based off of hard data and not someones “gut feeling”.
On the topic of variance, we see that each posterior has a different variance, and that the informative gamma distribution has an extremely small variance. This is due to the fact that the formula to get variance for a gamma distribution is alpha/lambda^2, we started with a very high lambda (in this case (k)) to begin with (1306), this denominator is squared to get a denominator of 1705636. Wheras the denominators of our betas don’t even breach 10000. Plus the numerators for beta distribution are also high since it relies on both alpha and beta.
In this mini project, findings show that the posteriors of proportion of Nadal points served includes 0.74 throughout. We find that as data is added to a prior, the posterior will settle towards its true value. A major surprising finidng in this project is that the uniformed beta(1, 1) prior has an almost identical posterior mean to the informative beta prior’s posterior mean.

Analysis of SE(Y_min) and SE(Y_max)
For the normal distribution the SE(Y_min) was 1.41 and the SE(Y_max) was 1.93. What is notable about this is that the two SE are relatively the same. Which makes sense because a normal distribution is generally symmetrical so our sampling distributions of Y_min and Y_max should have a relatively similar SE.
For the uniform distribution we see a similar result to the normal distribution. SE(Y_min) was 0.852 and SE(Y_max) was 0.857. This is expected since a uniform distribution is perfectly symmetrical and “uniform” throughout the entire distribution.
For the exponential distribution, we get our first big change from the normal and uniform results. For the exponential distribution we get an SE(Y_min) of 0.386 and an SE(Y_max) of 2.40. This makes sense since in an exponential distribution we get an extremely high amount of density around the lower end meaning our minimum doesn’t vary much. But, as you you continue towards infinity, we get little density and much more variance between maximums.
With the beta distribution we see almost a mix of results from the normal and exponential. We see anb SE(Y_min) of 0.104 and an SE(Y_max) of 0.0461. So the the SE(Y_min) and SE(Y_max) do appear to be relatively different, but not as much as the exponential. Which makes sense if we look at the beta distribution, we see a normal looking distribution with a left skew, which indicates more variance of the Y_min.
A general rule for SE(Y_min) and SE(Y_max) could be: If the distribution is symmetrical, the SE(Y_min) and SE(Y_max) should be relatively identical wheras a skewed distribution should have very different SE(Y_min) and SE(Y_max).
Question 2: PDF of Y_min and Y_max of Exponential distribution:
PDF of Exp(0.5) = 0.5 * exp(-0.5 * x) from 0 to infinity CDF of Exp(0.5) = 1 - exp(-0.5 * x) from 0 to infinity

n = 5
x = seq(0, 5, length.out = 1000)

## Y_min and Y_max densities using PDF and CDF above
density_min = n * ((-1 * exp(-0.5 * x))^4) * (0.5 * exp(-0.5 * x))
density_max = n * ((1 - exp(-0.5 * x))^4) * (0.5 * exp(-0.5 * x))

## Plotting the density of Y_min
EXPmin_df = tibble(x, density_min)
ggplot(data = EXPmin_df, aes(x = x, y = density_min)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal()







## Plotting the density of Y_max

ggplot(data = EXPmax_df, aes(x = x, y = density_max)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal()







## Integrating to find E(Y_min) and E(Y_max)
## Starting by making functions of the integrand
intY_min = function(y) {
  y * 5 * ((-1 * exp(-0.5 * y))^4) * (0.5 * exp(-0.5 * y))
}

intY_max = function(y) {
  y * 5 * ((1 - exp(-0.5 * y))^4) * (0.5 * exp(-0.5 * y))
}

## finding E(Y_min) and E(Y_max) via integrate() function

(EY_min = integrate(intY_min, 0, Inf))

0.4 with absolute error < 5.3e-05

(EY_max = integrate(intY_max, 0, Inf))

4.566667 with absolute error < 3.9e-05


The theoretical E(Y_min) is 0.4 and the theoretical E(Y_max) is 4.567. Our simulated model had E(Y_min) at 0.391 and E(Y_max) at 4.59. We see that the teoretical answers and the simulated answers for E(Y_min) and E(Y_max) are extremely close!
